turns.claim: AI is good for society overall because its benefits outweigh the risks when it is deployed responsibly, with governance and safeguards.
turns.reason: Turn 1 already claimed AI is good for society, but it supported that conclusion using benefits like convenience, health, accessibility, and safety; Turn 3 reaches the same conclusion through a different rebuttal-focused derivation based on jobs, education, bias, privacy, and responsible deployment.

turns.claim: AI is not overall good for society because its harms are built into the way it is developed and deployed, making proposed guardrails unreliable.
turns.reason: Turn 2 already argued AI is harmful overall, but it did so via jobs, critical thinking, bias, and privacy harms generally; Turn 4 reaches the same bottom-line conclusion through a different structural argument that mitigation measures cannot reliably fix those harms.

turns.claim: AI can be good for society overall if society uses enforceable structural guardrails and active constraints to manage risks.
turns.reason: Turn 3 already concluded that AI can be overall good and that valid risks require governance, but Turn 5 reaches that conclusion through a different derivation centered on structural regulation and enforceable deployment constraints rather than the earlier mix of mitigation, education, and privacy safeguards.

turns.claim: AI is societally harmful because it enables large-scale manipulation and misinformation that governance cannot reliably contain.
turns.reason: Turn 4 already claimed AI is harmful overall and that governance/mitigation is structurally insufficient, but it justified that mainly through labor displacement, dependence undermining critical thinking, bias, and privacy; Turn 6 reaches the same overall conclusion via a new mechanism centered on mass deception, propaganda, and amplified polarization.

turns.claim: AI can still be good for society overall because, even though it can amplify misinformation and manipulation, it can also help detect, verify, and mitigate those harms when governed responsibly.
turns.reason: Earlier turn 5 already concluded that AI is overall good if society uses enforceable guardrails, but this turn reaches that conclusion through a new derivation centered specifically on misinformation defenses, provenance tools, and AI-enabled countermeasures rather than the prior focus on general governance, health, jobs, and safety.

turns.claim: Even if AI can also defend against misinformation, those defenses are not symmetric or reliable enough in practice, because detection lags creation, provenance tools are brittle, and the burden of verification falls on ordinary people rather than bad actors, so AI remains socially harmful overall.
turns.reason: Turn 6 already argued that AI drives large-scale manipulation and misinformation and that governance cannot keep pace, but Turn 8 reaches the broader harmful-overall conclusion through a new mechanism: an arms-race asymmetry in verification and defense rather than the earlier focus on cheap mass deception and polarization.

turns.claim: AI can still be good for society overall because governance can shift misinformation-defense responsibility from ordinary people to platforms and deployers, using liability, provenance tools, and restrictions on high-risk uses.
turns.reason: Turn 7 made the same overall claim that AI can remain good despite misinformation risk, but it relied on AI also defending the information environment; Turn 9 reaches that conclusion through a different mechanism, namely structural governance that transfers verification burdens away from the public.

turns.claim: Even with platform liability, provenance/verification services, and restrictions on high-risk uses, AI still is not good for society overall because the main harms persist under realistic governance constraints and some defenses worsen privacy risks.
turns.reason: Turn 8 made the same overall claim that safeguards cannot make AI societally good, but it argued from an arms-race/verification-asymmetric misinformation dynamic; Turn 10 reaches that conclusion through a different mechanism centered on implementability of liability, surveillance costs of verification workflows, and continued attention/decision manipulation.

turns.claim: AI can be good for society overall because society can use tiered, targeted deployment to capture low-risk benefits while limiting high-risk uses.
turns.reason: Earlier turns already argued the same overall conclusion that AI can be good for society, but this turn reaches it through a new mechanism: stratified/tiered deployment that separates high-risk from low-risk uses, rather than the earlier emphasis on general responsible deployment, governance, or AI’s defensive uses against misinformation.

turns.claim: Tiered deployment or stratified AI rules cannot reliably separate safe from harmful uses, because mission creep, spillover, data/power concentration, and discriminatory everyday applications still make AI societally harmful in practice.
turns.reason: Turn 10 also argues that governance and selective restrictions fail to make AI overall good, but it relies mainly on platform liability, verification services, and privacy tradeoffs, whereas this turn’s derivation focuses on fragile risk boundaries, repurposing/mission creep, and harms spreading into ordinary contexts.

turns.claim: AI can still be net beneficial for society if society combines privacy-preserving design with market/capability controls to reduce surveillance, concentration, and mission creep while preserving gains in health, accessibility, education, and workplace safety.

turns.claim: AI can be good for society because its benefits are real and its harms are not unavoidable; they can be reduced through design choices, oversight, and policy.
turns.reason: Turn 1 already argued that AI is good for society, but this turn supports that conclusion with a different derivation centered on rebutting AG2’s specific harms and showing they can be mitigated through governance, worker protections, educational design, fairness audits, and privacy controls.

turns.claim: AI is not good for society overall because incentives, opacity, and weak accountability make “responsible deployment” unreliable and turn risks into real-world harm.
turns.reason: Turn 2 already concluded that AI is not good for society overall, but it relied mainly on direct harms like job loss, reduced critical thinking, bias, and privacy risk; Turn 4 reaches the same conclusion through a different mechanism centered on governance failure, black-box opacity, power asymmetry, and underfunded mitigation.

turns.claim: AI is good for society because its benefits are actionable and can be prioritized, and because risk can be reduced through governance mechanisms rather than making AI categorically bad.
turns.reason: Earlier Turn 3 made the same bottom-line claim that AI is good for society when responsibly governed, but this turn supports it with a different derivation focused on the counterfactual of rejecting AI, the limits of regulation, and governance mechanisms like auditing and recourse.

turns.claim: AI is not good for society overall because it amplifies manipulation, surveillance, and unequal harms faster than governance can contain.
turns.reason: Like Turn 4, it concludes AI is not good for society overall, but here the support shifts to qualitatively different harms—cheap deception/deepfakes, repurposable infrastructure, and irreversible harms—rather than opacity/accountability failures and weak mitigation.

turns.claim: AI is good for society because it offers real benefits in health, accessibility, and safety, and it can also be used defensively to reduce misinformation and fraud through verification and privacy safeguards.
turns.reason: Earlier turns already claimed AI is good for society, but this turn reaches that conclusion through a new emphasis on defensive anti-misinformation uses and the idea of reducing marginal harm with targeted governance, rather than mainly through productivity, access, healthcare, and counterfactual risk-reduction arguments.

turns.claim: AI is not good for society overall because defensive AI does not neutralize AI’s broader harms and instead entrenches the harmful system.
turns.reason: Turn 6 already claimed AI is not good for society overall, but it argued from AI’s expansion of manipulation, surveillance, and unequal harms; Turn 8 reaches the same conclusion through a different mechanism, namely that defensive AI creates an arms race that entrenches the very system causing harm.

turns.claim: AI can be good for society overall because its risks are manageable through safeguards, privacy-preserving defenses, and restricted deployment in high-value domains like health, accessibility, and workplace safety.
turns.reason: Like Turn 7, it defends the same overall conclusion that AI is good for society, but here the route is different: it emphasizes arms-race dynamics, privacy-preserving defensive tools, and controlled normalization/deployment rules rather than Turn 7’s focus on defensive AI, misinformation detection, and targeted governance.

turns.claim: AI is not good for society overall because profit incentives and fragmented accountability make safeguards like privacy-preserving design, provenance, staged rollouts, and strong rules only partial and temporary, so predictable harms keep scaling.
turns.reason: The conclusion that AI is not good for society overall matches earlier turns, especially Turn 4, but this turn reaches it through a new derivation focused on market incentives, minimum viable compliance, and regulatory capture rather than the earlier emphasis on opacity/accountability gaps or on manipulation/surveillance arms races.

turns.claim: AI is good for society because imperfect incentives can be managed with stronger enforceable governance, and society can still capture net benefits from AI in high-value areas like health, accessibility, and workplace safety.
turns.reason: Like Turn 9, it concludes AI is good for society despite AG2’s risk-based objections, but here the derivation is specifically that imperfect incentives are common in transformative technologies and can be addressed with liability, audits, procurement, and enforcement, rather than Turn 9’s focus on defensive AI, privacy-preserving design, and staged deployment.

turns.claim: AI is not good for society overall because its harms are systemic, hard to attribute, and scale faster than audits or liability can keep up, making regulation an unreliable stabilizer.
turns.reason: Earlier turns already concluded that AI is not good for society overall, but this turn reaches that conclusion through a different mechanism focused on opacity, causal uncertainty, continuous model change, and failed legal/audit accountability rather than the prior emphasis on incentives, regulatory capture, or defensive arms-race dynamics.

turns.claim: AI is good for society because accountability for its harms can be engineered through traceability, versioning, continuous audits, and procedural contestability, so hard governance problems do not justify concluding AI is not good overall.
turns.reason: Earlier AG1 turns already argued that AI is good for society, but this turn reaches that conclusion via a new accountability-focused mechanism—traceability, version control, continuous monitoring, and contestable procedures—rather than the prior emphasis on general benefits, governance, or staged rollout.
